extracted.intended_audience: students learning introductory algebraic geometry (advanced undergraduates/first-year graduate students); readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes
extracted.subtask_description: Define and analyze affine and projective varieties as topological spaces equipped with rings of regular functions (baby ringed spaces), including Zariski topology, coordinate rings, regular/rational functions, distinguished opens, graded rings, homogeneous ideals, and Hilbert functions/polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski closed sets
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Zariski topology on A^n, the closed sets are those of the form V(I) where I ⊆ C[x1, ..., xn].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open sets are complements of such sets. Examples: in A^1 closed sets are finite sets of points or all of A^1 (V(0)); in A^2 closed sets include curves like V(y−x^2) and single points like V(x−3,y−4). Note that nonempty Zariski open sets are "huge" (complements of finite unions of varieties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski topology axioms/properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection of V(I) satisfies ∅ and A^n are closed, arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed, and finite unions of closed sets are closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is justified because closed sets are affine varieties and varieties are closed under intersections and finite unions. Consequences: Zariski-open neighborhoods should be interpreted as 'true for virtually all points except those on certain curves'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguished open sets D(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: For V ⊆ A^n and f ∈ C[x1,...,xn], define D(f) = {p ∈ V | f(p) ≠ 0} = V \ V(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of D(f) as the 'doesn't-vanish set'. All open sets can be written as V \ V(I); if I = (f) is principal then the open set is a distinguished open. Properties: if (f) ⊆ (g) then D(f) ⊆ D(g); D(fg)=D(f)∩D(g). Examples: D(x) in A^1 is a line minus a point; D(x)∪D(y) = A^2 \ {(0,0)} is the punctured plane (not distinguished).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate ring C[V]
rubrics_metrics.description: The coordinate ring C[V] of a variety V is the ring of polynomial functions on V; if V = V(I) with I radical then C[V] ≅ C[x1,...,xn]/I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate functions x,y,z generate the ring; on V some polynomials coincide (e.g., on the parabola y−x^2 the functions y and x^2 agree), hence quotienting by I. Use the natural surjection C[x1,...,xn] ↠ C[V] whose kernel is I. Properties of V correspond to properties of C[V].

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational functions on open sets (affine)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational function on U ⊆ V is a quotient f(x)/g(x) of two elements f,g ∈ C[V] with g(x) ≠ 0 for x ∈ U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first natural notion, but it is too restrictive because the same function may require different representations on different local neighborhoods. Rational functions form the pool from which regular (locally rational) functions are built.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular functions (locally rational)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function ϕ: U → C is regular if for every p ∈ U there exists an open Up ⊆ U and a rational function fp/gp on Up with ϕ(x)=fp(x)/gp(x) for all x∈Up (and gp nonvanishing on Up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, regular = 'locally a rational function'. All elements of C[V] are regular (take gp=1). The local clause is necessary (Example 78.5.5) where globally writing a single quotient runs into divide-by-zero issues; this motivates sheafification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular functions on distinguished open sets (affine) — characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: If V ⊆ A^n is affine and D(g) a distinguished open subset, then OV(D(g)) = { f / g^k | f ∈ C[V], k ∈ Z≥0 }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular OV(V) = OV(D(1)) ≅ C[V]. The proof uses Nullstellensatz (hence requires algebraically closed base field C); the statement can fail over R (counterexample: 1/(x^2+1)). Sketch: locally represent ϕ, clear denominators on a cover, use Nullstellensatz to write a global power gn as a combination of local denominators, and form a global numerator f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baby ringed space
rubrics_metrics.description: A baby ringed space is a topological space X equipped with a ring OX(U) for every open set U, where elements of OX(U) are functions f: U → C (called regular functions on U).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affine varieties (V, OV) are examples of baby ringed spaces. The term is informal: in a full ringed space the rings need not literally be rings of functions U→C and must satisfy sheaf axioms; baby ringed space emphasizes the intuition without full technicalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graded ring
rubrics_metrics.description: A graded ring R decomposes as R = ⊕_{d≥0} R_d (as abelian groups) with multiplication R_d · R_e ⊆ R_{d+e}; elements of R_d are homogeneous of degree d. R+ = ⊕_{d>0} R_d is the irrelevant ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: polynomial ring C[x0,...,xn] graded by total degree, C[x] graded by degree. Remarks: in practice all graded rings here are commutative with 1; deg 0 for 0 is abusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal I ⊆ C[x0,...,xn] is homogeneous if it can be generated by homogeneous polynomials (equivalently I = ⊕_d (R_d ∩ I)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If I and J are homogeneous then I+J, IJ, I∩J, and √I are homogeneous. Homogeneous ideals are the natural objects for projective varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective vanishing locus Vpr(f) and projective variety
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is homogeneous, define Vpr(f) = { (x0:...:xn) | f(x0,...,xn)=0 }. A projective variety in CP^n is the common zero locus of an arbitrary collection of homogeneous polynomials in n+1 variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homogeneous condition is necessary (expressions like x0−1 are not well-defined on projective points). Use homogeneous ideals I to define Vpr(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevant ideal and its exceptionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal I = (x0, x1, ..., xn) (the irrelevant ideal) is a homogeneous radical ideal but its projective vanishing locus Vpr(I) = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an exception when setting up bijections between homogeneous radical ideals and projective varieties: exclude the irrelevant ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous Nullstellensatz
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I and J be homogeneous ideals. (a) If Vpr(I)=Vpr(J)≠∅ then √I = √J. (b) If Vpr(I)=∅ then either I=(1) or I=(x0,...,xn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus there is a bijection between projective varieties in CP^n and homogeneous radical ideals of C[x0,...,xn] except for the irrelevant ideal. Proof idea: pass to affine cones in A^{n+1} and apply the affine Nullstellensatz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous coordinate ring
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective variety V = Vpr(I) with I homogeneous radical, the homogeneous coordinate ring is C[V] = C[x0,...,xn]/I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: elements of C[V] do not directly define functions V → C, but rather functions on the affine cone V(I) ⊆ A^{n+1}. This motivates the additional homogeneity constraint in rational functions on projective varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational functions on projective varieties — same degree requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational function ϕ on U ⊆ V (projective) is a quotient f/g where f,g ∈ C[V] are homogeneous of the same degree and Vpr(g)∩U = ∅, giving a well-defined function U→C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equal-degree requirement ensures the value is well-defined on projective points (scaling cancels). Example: on CP^1, expressions like (s^2+9t^2)/t^2 equal (s/t)^2+9 on the affine chart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular functions on projective varieties (locally homogeneous quotients)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function ϕ: U→C is regular if for every p there exists Up containing p and a rational function fp/gp (with fp,gp homogeneous of same degree and gp nonvanishing on Up) such that ϕ=fp/gp on Up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors the affine sheaf definition but with the homogeneity constraint. Use these local representations to define the sheaf OV on projective varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular functions on distinguished open sets (projective) — characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Let V be projective and g ∈ C[V] homogeneous of positive degree. Then OV(D(g)) = { f / g^r | f ∈ C[V] homogeneous of degree r·deg g }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deg g > 0, D(g) 'looks affine' and the distinguished-open regular functions resemble the affine description. The result relies on comparing to the affine cone and uses similar Nullstellensatz arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only constant regular functions on irreducible projective variety
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is an irreducible projective variety then OV(V) ≅ C — the only global regular functions are constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses that the base field is algebraically closed (C). Irreducibility is necessary: e.g., a union of two points has OV(V) ≅ C⊕C and hence nonconstant global regular functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function of a homogeneous ideal / projective variety
rubrics_metrics.description: For homogeneous I ⊆ C[x0,...,xn], define h_I(d) = dim_C (C[x0,...,xn]/I)_d. For a projective variety V, set h_V = h_{Irad(V)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: h_I(d) measures the dimension of the degree-d piece of the coordinate ring. Examples: for the single point (0:0:1) in CP^2, h(d) ≡ 1; for the 'double point' ideal (x^2,y) the Hilbert function is 1 at d=0 and 2 for d≥1. For empty variety (irrelevant ideal) h_I(d)=0 for all sufficiently large d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity relation for Hilbert functions (I∩J and I+J)
rubrics_metrics.description: For homogeneous ideals I and J, h_{I∩J} + h_{I+J} = h_I + h_J (degreewise equality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a short exact sequence 0 → [S/(I∩J)]_d → [S/I]_d ⊕ [S/J]_d → [S/(I+J)]_d → 0 for each d and dimensions of finite-dimensional vector spaces. This relation is used to inductively compute Hilbert functions of unions of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function of zero-dimensional (finite) projective variety is eventually constant
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a projective variety consisting of m points (counted without necessarily being reduced), then h_V(d) = m for all sufficiently large d. More generally if dim V = 0 then h_I(d) is eventually constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction using the additivity relation and the fact that an ideal J with Vpr(J)=∅ has h_J(d)=0 for d≫0. Examples: two distinct points in CP^1 have Hilbert function equal to 2 for large d; the double point (nonreduced) also has eventual constant 2 (counting multiplicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function / polynomial behavior for projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: For CP^n, h_{CP^n}(d) = binomial(d+n, n) which is a polynomial in d of degree n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial proof via 'balls and urns' argument. This motivates the notion of Hilbert polynomial: for varieties of positive dimension the Hilbert function agrees with a polynomial (the Hilbert polynomial) for large d, whose degree is the dimension of the variety.
